title: A Three-level Framework for LLM-enhanced Explainable AI: From Technical Explanations to Natural Language
status: Journal article; supplied PDF accepted 19 November 2025, modified publication 2026; canonical year pending publisher verification
access_depth: Full supplied paper, sections 3–5 especially pp. 8–18
contribution: Three levels: algorithmic/domain evidence, human-centered interaction, societal transparency; LLM interprets existing XAI evidence for audiences.
limitations: Authors explicitly acknowledge conceptual foundation requiring further empirical validation (p.18); loan illustrations are not a controlled user study or measured faithfulness guarantee.
relevance: Primary audience-aware framework motivation; broad integration is already proposed.

title: Explaining machine learning models with interactive natural language conversations using TalkToModel
status: Published journal article per author repository citation; DOI verified in README, publisher page inaccessible
access_depth: Official README including abstract and citation; no full paper accessed
contribution: Adaptive dialogue engine interprets natural language, execution component constructs explanations, conversational interface presents them. Repository supports tabular models and includes diabetes, COMPAS, German credit demos.

title: InterroLang: Exploring NLP Models and Datasets through Dialogue-based Explanations
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2023
status: Published proceedings metadata verified in official ACL Anthology record
access_depth: Official ACL metadata abstract plus official README; full paper not accessed
contribution: Adapts TalkToModel to NLP; integrates feature attribution, counterfactuals/perturbations, free-text rationalization and dataset exploration. Official abstract reports two studies: perceived correctness/helpfulness and simulatability; dialogue explanations helped users predict hidden model labels more reliably than one-off explanations.
limitations: Perceived helpfulness and model simulatability are distinct from decision correctness and calibrated reliance. Results concern the studied models/tasks; detailed study protocol and effect sizes have not been read. Documented target models are BERT-family task classifiers, not evidence of verified explanations for instruction-tuned generative decision LLMs.
relevance: Very close system-level prior art: combining conversation, NLP attribution, counterfactuals and rationalization is not a new contribution by itself.
baseline_use: Source of operation taxonomy and NLP UX; compare verified final claims and explicit failure reporting if method differences warrant. No licence confirmed from root LICENSE URL (404).
license: Not verified; absence at one URL is not proof no licence exists
official_abstract: While recently developed NLP explainability methods let us open the black box in various ways (Madsen et al., 2022), a missing ingredient in this endeavor is an interactive tool offering a conversational interface. Such a dialogue system can help users explore datasets and models with explanations in a contextualized manner, e.g. via clarification or follow-up questions, and through a natural language interface. We adapt the conversational explanation framework TalkToModel (Slack et al., 2022) to the NLP domain, add new NLP-specific operations such as free-text rationalization, and illustrate its generalizability on three NLP tasks (dialogue act classification, question answering, hate speech detection). To recognize user queries for explanations, we evaluate fine-tuned and few-shot prompting models and implement a novel adapter-based approach. We then conduct two user studies on (1) the perceived correctness and helpfulness of the dialogues, and (2) the simulatability, i.e. how objectively helpful dialogical explanations are for humans in figuring out the model’s predicted label when it’s not shown. We found rationalization and feature attribution were helpful in explaining the model behavior. Moreover, users could more reliably predict the model outcome based on an explanation dialogue rather than one-off explanations.

title: On Evaluating Explanation Utility for Human-AI Decision Making in NLP
status: Published proceedings metadata verified in official ACL Anthology record
access_depth: Official ACL metadata abstract plus official README and study-template index; full paper not accessed
contribution: Reviews application-grounded explanation evaluation metrics and dataset-selection criteria; abstract reports only 4 of more than 50 considered explainability datasets satisfy their criteria. On legal-claim verification given contracts, AI predictions with or without explanations did not speed decision-makers without compromising performance. Argues for revisiting team design and deferral.
limitations: Task-specific negative result cannot be generalized to every explanation or application. The abstract does not show that explanations are always useless; full protocol/effect sizes remain uninspected. Highlights need for tasks where human-AI teams are meaningful, independent outcome measurement and appropriate deferral.
relevance: Direct evaluation-design prior art for thesis human study and suitable decision-support domains; should be read in full before selecting protocol.
baseline_use: Protocol and human-study design source rather than explanation-generation algorithm baseline.
official_abstract: Is explainability a false promise? This debate has emerged from the insufficient evidence that explanations help people in situations they are introduced for. More human-centered, application-grounded evaluations of explanations are needed to settle this. Yet, with no established guidelines for such studies in NLP, researchers accustomed to standardized proxy evaluations must discover appropriate measurements, tasks, datasets, and sensible models for human-AI teams in their studies. To aid with this, we first review existing metrics suitable for application-grounded evaluation. We then establish criteria to select appropriate datasets, and using them, we find that only 4 out of over 50 datasets available for explainability research in NLP meet them. We then demonstrate the importance of reassessing the state of the art to form and study human-AI teams: teaming people with models for certain tasks might only now start to make sense, and for others, it remains unsound. Finally, we present the exemplar studies of human-AI decision-making for one of the identified tasks — verifying the correctness of a legal claim given a contract. Our results show that providing AI predictions, with or without explanations, does not cause decision makers to speed up their work without compromising performance. We argue for revisiting the setup of human-AI teams and improving automatic deferral of instances to AI, where explanations could play a useful role.

title: Reframing Human-AI Collaboration for Generating Free-Text Explanations
status: Published proceedings metadata verified in official ACL Anthology record
access_depth: Official ACL abstract and metadata plus official README; full paper not accessed
contribution: Few-shot GPT3 free-text explanation generation combined with a supervised filter using binary human acceptability judgments. Official abstract reports crowdworkers sometimes prefer generated explanations to dataset human explanations, with weaknesses including novel information and support for the label.
limitations: Human acceptability is partly correlated with fine-grained explanation attributes, not proof of mechanistic faithfulness. Preference and grammatical/factual sufficiency need not imply appropriate reliance; full study protocol and effect sizes not read.

baseline_use: Human acceptability annotation materials and methodological background; investigate before reusing datasets/prompts.

title: Attribute-Based Activation Steering of LLMs for Group-Specific Explanation Generation
venue: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
status: Published October 2026 proceedings metadata in official ACL Anthology; peer-review venue citation also in official repo
access_depth: Official ACL metadata/abstract plus official research README; no full paper accessed
official_abstract: To effectively enable people to understand new topics, explanations should be tailored to their backgrounds and abilities. Prompting alone has been shown to be insufficient for creating such explanations, and other computational methods are missing so far. Therefore, this paper investigates whether LLMs can be steered to generate explanations that are tailored to a specific group of people. To this end, we propose an approach that first identifies group-specific attributes in terms of explanatory style and knowledge of a specific target group. Building on activation engineering, it then computes attribute-based steering vectors and adds them to the internal activations of an LLM during inference to enable a fine-grained steering. In our experiments, we assess the steering effectiveness in terms of specificity and factuality of the generated explanations. Additionally, we evaluate the explanations in a study with human experts from different target groups. Compared to prompting and state-of-the-art steering baselines, our approach tailors the explanations significantly better to the target group while maintaining the best specificity-factuality balance.
contribution: Identifies target-group style/knowledge attributes, computes attribute-based activation steering vectors and adds them during LLM inference. Abstract reports evaluation of group specificity, factuality and human experts compared with prompting/steering baselines; claimed better specificity-factuality balance is author-reported abstract evidence.
limitations: Group-specific topic explanation and factuality are not the same as faithful explanation of a target classifier decision. No full-paper protocol/effect sizes inspected. Requires white-box activation access and more infrastructure than simple prompting; README says full generated database exceeds 100 GB with only an exemplary subset shared.
relevance: Very direct, recent prior art: audience tailoring with factuality evaluation cannot be claimed first-ever. Promising narrower question: preservation of verified target-model evidence across audience adaptation, assessed separately from encyclopedic factuality.
baseline_use: Adaptation baseline or related method; compare prompting-based audience variants first if steering implementation is beyond available compute. Do not imply head-to-head reproduction already run.
